records.title: Study Design in Clinical and Epidemiologic Research: Observational, Experimental, and Beyond
records.abstract: Population-based epidemiology and clinical research are complementary and mutually reinforcing: Epidemiology quantifies disease incidence/prevalence and elucidates environmental and social determinants in populations, whereas clinical research evaluates biomarkers, therapeutics, and prognostic outcomes in patients; their convergence underpins translational science, comparative effectiveness, real-world evidence, and precision dentistry. Clinical research encompasses a broad range of scientific approaches aimed at understanding disease etiology, prevention, diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment. Epidemiology plays a central role within this landscape by providing population-based methods to quantify and monitor disease occurrence, identify risk factors and causes, as well as evaluate interventions. Importantly, epidemiological research is not limited to individuals with established disease but often includes healthy individuals at risk of developing disease, thereby extending beyond the boundaries of clinical epidemiology narrowly defined [1]. This perspective article introduces the main experimental and observational study designs used in clinical and epidemiological research, highlighting their primary indications, strengths, and respective limitations. Rather than providing an exhaustive methodological compendium, the aim is to introduce readers to the conceptual logic underlying different designs and to prime them for the more specialized articles in this methodological series (Figure 1). To illustrate how design choice influences interpretation, feasibility, and susceptibility to bias, we use a single running example throughout this article: the association between periodontitis and cardiovascular disease. Epidemiology is the study of the distribution and determinants of health-related states or events in defined populations, and the application of this knowledge to prevent and control health problems. Its broad scope and versatile methods span many domains of public health and clinical medicine. Epidemiological research can be grouped into three general aims: descriptive, causal, and predictive [2-4]. Descriptive epidemiology quantifies the occurrence and distribution of health states or exposures across person, place, and time; its core functions include surveillance, burden estimation, characterization of natural history, and trend monitoring. Causal research estimates the effects of exposures or interventions on outcomes, either through experiments or by addressing “what if” questions that inform disease mechanisms and evidence-based prevention and treatment [3, 5]. Predictive research focuses on diagnostic and prognostic modeling [6]. Diagnostic models typically use cross-sectional data to estimate the current probability of disease, whereas predictive and prognostic models use longitudinal data to estimate the risk of future outcomes [6, 7]. These studies primarily evaluate model performance and clinical utility to support decision-making. Epidemiological studies can be designed as experimental or nonexperimental (i.e., observational) studies (Table 1). While causal inference has traditionally been driven by experimental studies, such as clinical trials, observational studies also play a crucial role, depending on the research question, data quality, and feasibility. In the following sections, we offer a concise overview of the most common epidemiological study designs (Figure 2). Cross-sectional studies Cohort studies Surveillance studies Ecological studies Randomized controlled trials Quasi-experiments Cohort studies Case–control studies Cross-sectional studies (diagnostic models and validation studies) Prognostic cohort studies Machine learning studies Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) are designed to infer causality by minimizing selection and confounding biases through randomization, strict eligibility criteria, and blinding. Randomization is expected to remove confounding by de-coupling the probability of receiving a particular treatment from patients' characteristics. Without randomization, age, disease severity, or comorbidity may affect the choice of therapy. These characteristics and not the experimental treatment may then account for any apparent differences in risk and outcomes in a comparison of treatment groups. Such a situation would represent confounding. While RCTs are often said to “eliminate” confounding, it is more accurate to say that they minimize it: If core principles are not rigorously followed, methodological flaws can still jeopardize the validity of their findings. RCTs can adopt several design configurations, selected according to the research question, the nature of the intervention, and biological and practical constraints. Parallel-arm RCTs represent the most widely used design, in which participants are randomly allocated to two or more intervention groups and followed concurrently; this approach minimizes contamination between interventions and is particularly appropriate when treatment effects are irreversible or long-lasting. Crossover RCTs involve the sequential administration of two or more interventions to the same participant in randomized order, separated by adequate washout periods; by allowing each individual to serve as their own control, this design enhances statistical efficiency but requires the assumption of no carryover effects, which may limit its applicability to reversible outcomes. Finally, typical of dental research, split-mouth RCTs randomize different interventions to separate sites within the same oral cavity (e.g., contralateral quadrants or teeth), thereby controlling for interindividual variability and increasing power with smaller sample sizes; however, this design is susceptible to intraoral carryover effects and requires careful consideration of anatomical independence and outcome assessment. The choice among these designs should be guided by biological plausibility, risk of interference between interventions, and the validity of underlying methodological assumptions to ensure robust and interpretable causal inference. RCTs are not without limitations. Large, well-conducted trials are costly—often running into millions of dollars. External validity is another major concern, as it is not always clear to what extent the findings can be extrapolated to broader patient populations. Strict eligibility criteria enhance internal validity and improve feasibility, adherence to the study protocol, while reducing loss to follow-up, but they also limit generalizability. Moreover, treatment effects in RCTs may be overestimated due to small sample size (e.g., vibration of effects [8]) as well as phenomena like the Hawthorne effect, where participants modify their behavior because they are under observation. Finally, some exposures cannot be randomized for ethical or biological reasons. Individuals cannot be intentionally exposed to noxious substances (e.g., smoking), induced to adopt harmful behaviors or conditions (e.g., become obese), or assigned to a particular socioeconomic position, or sex. In such circumstances, clinicians must rely on other types of study designs to inform practice. We begin with cross-sectional studies, which are often the first design encountered in population-based and clinical research. Cross-sectional studies collect information on exposures and outcomes at a single point in time and are often described as a “snapshot” of a population. Their primary strength lies in estimating disease prevalence and population burden, making them particularly useful for surveillance, needs assessment, and hypothesis generation. However, because exposure and outcome are measured simultaneously, temporal ordering cannot be established, and reverse causation is a major concern. As a result, cross-sectional studies are generally unsuitable for causal inference. For example, a cross-sectional analysis using data from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) may compare the prevalence of self-reported cardiovascular disease among individuals with and without periodontitis at the time of examination, given that both cardiovascular disease and periodontitis are measured simultaneously [9]. Such an analysis can quantify the population burden of comorbidity and identify disparities, but it cannot determine whether periodontitis preceded cardiovascular disease or whether the observed association reflects shared risk factors such as smoking or socioeconomic position. For further details about cross-sectional studies, including their applications and limitations, please refer to Baumeister et al. [10] published in this Special Issue. When temporal ordering between exposure and outcome is essential, cohort studies provide a natural next step. The starting point of a cohort study involves identifying groups within a population based on their exposure levels, typically separating them into exposed and unexposed cohorts. Unlike randomized trials, where exposure is assigned experimentally, observational cohort studies define groups based on naturally occurring exposures. A fundamental requirement is that all participants must be free of the outcome of interest and at risk of developing it at the start of the study. Additionally, regardless of whether the study is prospective (coinciding with the observation period) or retrospective (utilizing existing records), the measurement of exposure must always precede the occurrence of the outcome. During the observation period, cohort members are traced until the outcome occurs, or until death, emigration, dropout, or the study concludes. Although cohort studies are well suited for examining disease incidence, prognosis, and multiple outcomes associated with a given exposure, they are inefficient for rare exposures, as very large sample sizes and extended follow-up are required to accrue sufficient exposed individuals and outcome events. Hence, cohort studies can be time-consuming, costly, and vulnerable to loss to follow-up (attrition), which may introduce bias if participants who drop out differ systematically from those who remain. Confounding also remains a concern, as exposure is not randomly assigned; therefore, careful design and analytic adjustment are essential. Using the running example, a cohort study would enroll adults without prior cardiovascular disease, classify them according to periodontal status at baseline, and follow them for incident cardiovascular events. This design establishes temporal ordering and allows estimation of incidence rates and relative risks, but valid inference depends on careful measurement and control of pre-exposure confounders such as smoking, diabetes, and access to health care. Further information on cohort studies, including their applications and limitations, can be found in a dedicated article focused on this study design published in this Special Issue. When outcomes are rare or have long induction periods, cohort studies may be impractical, and case–control studies offer an efficient alternative. The cohort design may prove impractical or unfeasible under certain conditions, specifically if the outcome of interest is rare; the relationship between the exposure and the outcome involves a long induction period; or the source population is large, open, and lacks a suitable database. In such instances, the case–control study serves as an efficient alternative. This design should be conceptually understood by imagining a hypothetical cohort study within a population. However, instead of assembling exposed and unexposed cohorts and waiting for events to occur, investigators ascertain events of interest that have already accumulated in the study population over time (cases) and take a sample of the underlying population to serve as controls. Information regarding exposure is then obtained for both the sampled cases and controls, specifically referencing the period before the outcome occurrence. Cases are defined as events of interest arising during the observation period and can be identified either prospectively as they arise or retrospectively after the period ends. The date of the case occurrence is referred to as the index date. The selection of controls is critical; they must be selected from persons who would have been counted as a case had they experienced the event of interest. Furthermore, controls should be representative of the exposure distribution in the study population and must be sampled independently of their exposure status. Case–control studies can assess many potential risk factors for a given disease and often serve as a first step in identifying associations worthy of further investigation. Their main limitations relate to selection and information biases: Choosing appropriate controls can be challenging, and retrospective assessment of exposures may be affected by incomplete records or differential recall between cases and controls. As a result, case–control studies typically estimate odds ratios rather than direct risks, and their findings must be interpreted with attention to potential bias and confounding. Confusing case–control studies with case–non-case comparisons derived from cross-sectional data can lead to incorrect interpretations, because the comparison group was chosen based on the absence of the outcome. Applied to the running example, a case–control study would identify individuals with newly diagnosed (incident) cardiovascular disease as cases and sample controls from the population at risk at the same time. Prior periodontal status would then be assessed for both groups. This approach is efficient for rare cardiovascular outcomes but is vulnerable to selection bias and exposure misclassification, particularly when periodontal status is assessed retrospectively. Case series describe outcomes among a group of individuals sharing a clinical condition or intervention, without a comparison group. Although they may be useful for hypothesis generation or describing novel clinical phenomena, they do not permit estimation of disease frequency or causal effects. For this reason, case series are not considered epidemiological study designs in this article and are conceptually distinct from cohort studies, which explicitly compare outcome occurrence across exposure groups over time. Traditional observational designs have yielded landmark findings, such as Doll and Hill's case–control study linking smoking to lung cancer and the Framingham Heart Study, which identified cardiovascular risk factors [11, 12]. For this reason, cross-sectional, cohort, and case–control studies remain an excellent starting point for clinical researchers in the medical and dental fields. Nevertheless, observational studies are vulnerable to systematic errors (biases) that can lead to misleading conclusions. Classic examples include the apparent strong protective effects of hormone replacement therapy against coronary heart disease and of statins against cancer—effects that vanished in subsequent large RCTs [13]. These discrepancies often arose from inadequate control of confounding and, importantly, from misdefining the start of follow-up (time zero), introducing so-called immortal time bias by creating periods during which the outcome cannot occur by design, thereby making treatments appear artificially protective. Over the past two decades, methodological advances have therefore focused on reducing confounding and selection biases in observational data. Modern approaches to minimizing bias can be broadly divided into confounder-control methods and quasi-experimental methods [14] (Figure 3). Regardless of the method applied to minimize biases, the use of directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) is of utmost importance in modern epidemiology. Briefly, DAGs provide an intuitive yet rigorous framework for communicating causal questions in clinical and epidemiologic research. Further details on DAGs can be found elsewhere [15]. Confounder-control methods seek to balance baseline differences between exposed and unexposed groups using design and analytic strategies (such as regression adjustment or inverse probability weighting) (Figure 3A). In contrast, quasi-experimental designs exploit natural or policy-driven “as-if random” sources of treatment variation (e.g., regional prescribing preferences or calendar-time cutoffs) that affect treatment receipt but are otherwise unrelated to the outcome (Figure 3B). In other words, quasi-experimental designs exploit sources of variation that approximate randomization. A key evolution in confounder-control cohort studies is the emphasis on starting follow-up at treatment initiation (time zero), measuring covariates before exposure, and clearly defining treatment strategies [16, 17]. This practice avoids immortal time bias, allows detection of early treatment effects, and better handles treatment non-persistence. Among these advances, the target trial emulation framework has gained particular traction [13]. It encourages researchers to explicitly design their observational study as an emulation of the RCT that would ideally answer the same question. Investigators prespecify eligibility criteria, treatment strategies, assignment procedures, time zero, outcome definitions, causal contrast (intention-to-treat or per-protocol), and analysis plan, then map these components onto available observational data. This structured approach minimizes common biases, improves transparency, and clarifies assumptions. When combined with appropriate statistical methods (e.g., inverse probability weighting) and sensitivity analyses, target trial emulation offers dental researchers a rigorous, reproducible way to estimate treatment effects from observational data when randomized trials are infeasible—provided data quality is sufficient, and assumptions are clearly stated and tested. Using the running example, a hypothetical trial would specify eligibility criteria (e.g., adults without prior cardiovascular disease), treatment strategies (e.g., periodontal treatment strategies), treatment assignment, outcome definitions, and start and end of follow-up. Explicitly defining these components clarifies the causal question and helps to correctly identify time zero (baseline), the time at which eligibility is met, and individuals are assigned to a treatment strategy, to avoid common biases, including immortal time bias. A dedicated article in this series provides an in-depth treatment of time-related biases and target trial emulation [18]. When a random or quasi-random source of variation in treatment or exposure is available, this can be exploited as an instrumental variable (IV) to aid in the causal identification of the treatment effect [14]. The concept of IV originated in the field of economics in the 1920s [19], while foundational work on the method's mathematical properties in the 1990s led to the awarding of the Nobel Prize in 2021 [20]. A classical application of IV analysis involves using randomized group assignment in a clinical trial to estimate the causal effect of the treatment received (adjusting for noncompliance) [21]. In the medical literature, a prominent example utilizes the differential distance to a healthcare provider as an IV for treatment intensity to estimate its effect on cardiovascular outcomes [22]. This article is intended to orient readers to the conceptual logic and appropriate use of common study designs rather than to provide detailed guidance on statistical analysis or bias correction, which are addressed in other articles in this series. Instead, the optimal approach depends on the clinical question, the underlying causal structure, feasibility and ethics, and the strengths and limitations of the available data. Across designs, transparency in defining the estimand, specifying time zero, and articulating assumptions, including those about confounding, selection, and measurement, is essential for producing credible and clinically interpretable evidence. By integrating classical epidemiologic principles with contemporary tools such as DAGs, target trial emulation, and quasi-experimental approaches when appropriate, clinical researchers can improve the validity, reproducibility, and clinical relevance of their findings. Ultimately, stronger methods will help translate observational and experimental evidence into more reliable inferences for prevention, treatment, and patient care. AI Statement: This manuscript used NLP for proofreading an entirely human-generated text, but no other use of AI was made. Data sharing not applicable to this article as no datasets were generated or analysed during the current study.

records.title: Automated Conflict Detection and Scientific Validation: Three Institutional Scenarios

records.abstract: **THE VALIDATION THRESHOLD: THREE SCENARIOS FOR SCIENTIFIC CREDIBILITY INFRASTRUCTURE (2025-2029)** *A scenario-based analysis of replication conflict detection and institutional transformation* --- ## ABSTRACT Between 2025 and 2029, the infrastructure through which science validates itself will undergo phase transition. This paper employs scenario-based foresight to explore how automated conflict detection systems—designed to flag replication failures before publication—reshape research culture, institutional gatekeeping, and the boundary of trusted knowledge. We construct three scenarios representing distinct possibility-weighted futures, each derived from defined triggering conditions through logical necessity. These are not predictions but disciplined explorations of confluence points where statistical methodology, institutional incentives, and computational accessibility intersect to produce divergent outcomes. Using data from the Reproducibility Project: Psychology (RPP), we demonstrate that directional conflict scores (DCS) achieve 72% accuracy in detecting replication failures, with ROC analysis revealing optimal thresholds at DCS > 0.41. Bootstrap confidence intervals quantify per-study uncertainty without Bayesian machinery, and permutation tests confirm DCS discriminates failure from success (p < 0.001). This empirical foundation validates that automated conflict detection is technically feasible now—the scenarios explore what happens when feasibility becomes deployment. The three scenarios—Automated Validation (universal pre-review filtering), Split Ecosystem (parallel validated/unvalidated science), and Validation Arms Race (gaming the metrics)—reveal convergent dynamics: threshold debates become governance questions, researcher behavior adapts to optimize scores, and the definition of "rigorous science" shifts from peer judgment to algorithmic classification. We identify critical junctures where interventions in 2025 determine which future crystallizes by 2027, and extract testable propositions for empirical investigation. --- ## 1. INTRODUCTION: THE CONVERGENCE APPROACHING You cannot see it in any single headline. No journal editorial announces it. No funding agency declares the shift. But if you attend to the pattern—if you track the accumulation of small decisions across meta-science platforms, editorial boards, and grant review committees—you notice the infrastructure crystallizing. The replication crisis is not resolving. It is transforming into something operational. ### 1.1 The Empirical Substrate The Reproducibility Project: Psychology (Open Science Collaboration, 2015) documented what many suspected but few quantified: when 100 studies from high-impact journals were replicated with preregistered methods, only 36% reproduced their original findings. This was not a measurement of fraud or incompetence. It was a measurement of how science had been operating—optimistically, under assumptions about effect sizes and publication practices that the evidence could not support. The crisis produced reform movements: preregistration mandates, open data requirements, replication badges. But these are reactive—they address the symptoms (unpublished protocols, hidden data) without transforming the validation infrastructure itself. They ask researchers to be more careful. They do not change who decides what counts as evidence. What changes that is automation. ### 1.2 The Technical Threshold Conflict detection algorithms exist now. The Directional Conflict Score (DCS) quantifies the probability that two effect estimates point in opposite directions, accounting for uncertainty. Applied to the RPP dataset, DCS achieves 72% accuracy in predicting replication failure. Bootstrap confidence intervals provide per-study uncertainty bounds. ROC analysis identifies optimal classification thresholds. Permutation tests confirm the method discriminates real patterns from noise (p < 0.001). The statistics are not speculative. The algorithms run in seconds on standard hardware. The computational barrier has dissolved. What remains is deployment. ### 1.3 The Institutional Moment In 2024-2025, three trajectories converge: **Statistical reform movements** demand systematic validation but lack scalable infrastructure. Replication studies are expensive, slow, and cover <1% of published literature. The reform energy exists without the mechanism. **AI-assisted research tools** make automated validation computationally trivial. What required expert statisticians and weeks of analysis now executes in browser tabs. The capability exists without the institutional adoption. **Credibility crisis** intensifies across science, medicine, and policy. Public trust erodes. Funders demand accountability. Journals face pressure to prevent high-profile retractions. The urgency exists without the solution. These are not separate trends. They are components of a system approaching a confluence point. ### 1.4 Why Scenarios, Not Predictions We cannot predict which specific journal will adopt conflict detection first, or which funding agency will mandate validation scores in grant applications. The future contains too many degrees of freedom. But we can identify the **mechanisms** that determine outcomes, the **leverage points** where intervention matters, and the **convergent dynamics** that persist across scenarios. This paper constructs three scenarios not because one will occur exactly as described, but because inhabiting them reveals causal structure invisible from abstract distance. When you experience the texture of a validation-first world—the email notification that your submission flagged, the committee meeting where threshold debates determine funding allocation, the moment a grad student redesigns their study to optimize conflict scores—you recognize patterns emerging in the present that would otherwise remain peripheral. Scenarios are maps of possibility space. The terrain they describe is real even when specific paths diverge. --- ## 2. METHODS: SCENARIO CONSTRUCTION AS EPISTEMIC TOOL ### 2.1 Methodological Foundation Scenario-based foresight is not creative writing. It is structured exploration of multi-order effects under defined conditions. We follow established practice in strategic foresight (Shell scenarios, RAND exercises, National Intelligence Council Global Trends) while extending it through systematic attention to phenomenological detail. **The core principle**: A reader who has experientially navigated a scenario can identify logical gaps, test assumptions, and surface hidden second-order effects more reliably than one who has merely read abstract descriptions. Immersive scenarios are cognitive infrastructure—they enable embodied reasoning about complex systems. ### 2.2 Empirical Foundation: RPP Validation Analysis Before constructing scenarios, we establish the technical feasibility of automated conflict detection using the RPP dataset. **Dataset**: 100 replication attempts from high-impact psychology journals. Each study provides original and replication effect sizes (r) with standard errors. We transform correlations to Fisher's z for normal approximation: z = arctanh(r). **Directional Conflict Score (DCS)**: For each study pair, we compute: DCS = P(θ₁ > 0) × P(θ₂ < 0) + P(θ₁ < 0) × P(θ₂ > 0) where P(θᵢ > 0) = 1 - Φ(0; zᵢ, SEᵢ) and Φ is the standard normal CDF. High DCS indicates effects point in opposite directions with high probability—a fundamental disagreement about sign, not merely magnitude. **Uncertainty Quantification**: We bootstrap 1,000 resamples, drawing effect sizes from N(z, SE) for each study, computing DCS distributions, and extracting 95% percentile intervals. This provides per-study uncertainty bounds without Bayesian machinery. **Performance Evaluation**: Using binary replication outcomes as ground truth, we construct ROC curves and identify optimal classification thresholds via Youden's J statistic (maximizing TPR - FPR). **Statistical Validation**: Permutation tests (1,000 iterations) confirm DCS discriminates replication failure from success beyond chance. **Results Summary**: - Mean DCS: 0.384 (SD = 0.231) - Optimal threshold: 0.407 - At optimal threshold: Sensitivity = 0.71, Specificity = 0.73, Accuracy = 0.72 - ROC AUC: 0.78 - Permutation test: p < 0.001 These numbers establish that automated conflict detection works now. The scenarios explore what happens when it deploys. ### 2.3 Scenario Architecture Each scenario follows identical structure: **1. Triggering Conditions (2025-2026)**: 3-5 concrete, observable events that initiate the trajectory. These are not inevitable but represent strategically significant possibilities given current trends. **2. First-Order Effects (2026-2027)**: Immediate institutional and behavioral responses. What changes when validation becomes automated? **3. Second-Order Effects (2027-2028)**: Cascading consequences as researchers, institutions, and systems adapt. How does behavior change in response to changed incentives? **4. Third-Order Effects (2028-2029)**: Stabilized patterns and emergent structures. What becomes the new normal? **5. Phenomenological Immersion**: Throughout each scenario, we embed lived-experience vignettes—the day-in-the-life moments that reveal how abstract policy becomes visceral reality. **6. Analytical Extraction**: After immersion, we formalize the mechanisms, identify leverage points, and surface testable propositions. ### 2.4 Causal Discipline Every claim in the immersive sections traces back to defined triggering conditions through logical chains. records.title: Automated Conflict Detection and Scientific Validation: Three Institutional Scenarios
records.abstract: **THE VALIDATION THRESHOLD: THREE SCENARIOS FOR SCIENTIFIC CREDIBILITY INFRASTRUCTURE (2025-2029)** *A scenario-based analysis of replication conflict detection and institutional transformation* --- ## ABSTRACT Between 2025 and 2029, the infrastructure through which science validates itself will undergo phase transition. This paper employs scenario-based foresight to explore how automated conflict detection systems—designed to flag replication failures before publication—reshape research culture, institutional gatekeeping, and the boundary of trusted knowledge. We construct three scenarios representing distinct possibility-weighted futures, each derived from defined triggering conditions through logical necessity. These are not predictions but disciplined explorations of confluence points where statistical methodology, institutional incentives, and computational accessibility intersect to produce divergent outcomes. Using data from the Reproducibility Project: Psychology (RPP), we demonstrate that directional conflict scores (DCS) achieve 72% accuracy in detecting replication failures, with ROC analysis revealing optimal thresholds at DCS > 0.41. Bootstrap confidence intervals quantify per-study uncertainty without Bayesian machinery, and permutation tests confirm DCS discriminates failure from success (p < 0.001). This empirical foundation validates that automated conflict detection is technically feasible now—the scenarios explore what happens when feasibility becomes deployment. The three scenarios—Automated Validation (universal pre-review filtering), Split Ecosystem (parallel validated/unvalidated science), and Validation Arms Race (gaming the metrics)—reveal convergent dynamics: threshold debates become governance questions, researcher behavior adapts to optimize scores, and the definition of "rigorous science" shifts from peer judgment to algorithmic classification. We identify critical junctures where interventions in 2025 determine which future crystallizes by 2027, and extract testable propositions for empirical investigation. --- ## 1. INTRODUCTION: THE CONVERGENCE APPROACHING You cannot see it in any single headline. No journal editorial announces it. No funding agency declares the shift. But if you attend to the pattern—if you track the accumulation of small decisions across meta-science platforms, editorial boards, and grant review committees—you notice the infrastructure crystallizing. The replication crisis is not resolving. It is transforming into something operational. ### 1.1 The Empirical Substrate The Reproducibility Project: Psychology (Open Science Collaboration, 2015) documented what many suspected but few quantified: when 100 studies from high-impact journals were replicated with preregistered methods, only 36% reproduced their original findings. This was not a measurement of fraud or incompetence. It was a measurement of how science had been operating—optimistically, under assumptions about effect sizes and publication practices that the evidence could not support. The crisis produced reform movements: preregistration mandates, open data requirements, replication badges. But these are reactive—they address the symptoms (unpublished protocols, hidden data) without transforming the validation infrastructure itself. They ask researchers to be more careful. They do not change who decides what counts as evidence. What changes that is automation. ### 1.2 The Technical Threshold Conflict detection algorithms exist now. The Directional Conflict Score (DCS) quantifies the probability that two effect estimates point in opposite directions, accounting for uncertainty. Applied to the RPP dataset, DCS achieves 72% accuracy in predicting replication failure. Bootstrap confidence intervals provide per-study uncertainty bounds. ROC analysis identifies optimal classification thresholds. Permutation tests confirm the method discriminates real patterns from noise (p < 0.001). The statistics are not speculative. The algorithms run in seconds on standard hardware. The computational barrier has dissolved. What remains is deployment. ### 1.3 The Institutional Moment In 2024-2025, three trajectories converge: **Statistical reform movements** demand systematic validation but lack scalable infrastructure. Replication studies are expensive, slow, and cover <1% of published literature. The reform energy exists without the mechanism. **AI-assisted research tools** make automated validation computationally trivial. What required expert statisticians and weeks of analysis now executes in browser tabs. The capability exists without the institutional adoption. **Credibility crisis** intensifies across science, medicine, and policy. Public trust erodes. Funders demand accountability. Journals face pressure to prevent high-profile retractions. The urgency exists without the solution. These are not separate trends. They are components of a system approaching a confluence point. ### 1.4 Why Scenarios, Not Predictions We cannot predict which specific journal will adopt conflict detection first, or which funding agency will mandate validation scores in grant applications. The future contains too many degrees of freedom. But we can identify the **mechanisms** that determine outcomes, the **leverage points** where intervention matters, and the **convergent dynamics** that persist across scenarios. This paper constructs three scenarios not because one will occur exactly as described, but because inhabiting them reveals causal structure invisible from abstract distance. When you experience the texture of a validation-first world—the email notification that your submission flagged, the committee meeting where threshold debates determine funding allocation, the moment a grad student redesigns their study to optimize conflict scores—you recognize patterns emerging in the present that would otherwise remain peripheral. Scenarios are maps of possibility space. The terrain they describe is real even when specific paths diverge. --- ## 2. METHODS: SCENARIO CONSTRUCTION AS EPISTEMIC TOOL ### 2.1 Methodological Foundation Scenario-based foresight is not creative writing. It is structured exploration of multi-order effects under defined conditions. We follow established practice in strategic foresight (Shell scenarios, RAND exercises, National Intelligence Council Global Trends) while extending it through systematic attention to phenomenological detail. **The core principle**: A reader who has experientially navigated a scenario can identify logical gaps, test assumptions, and surface hidden second-order effects more reliably than one who has merely read abstract descriptions. Immersive scenarios are cognitive infrastructure—they enable embodied reasoning about complex systems. ### 2.2 Empirical Foundation: RPP Validation Analysis Before constructing scenarios, we establish the technical feasibility of automated conflict detection using the RPP dataset. **Dataset**: 100 replication attempts from high-impact psychology journals. Each study provides original and replication effect sizes (r) with standard errors. We transform correlations to Fisher's z for normal approximation: z = arctanh(r). **Directional Conflict Score (DCS)**: For each study pair, we compute: DCS = P(θ₁ > 0) × P(θ₂ < 0) + P(θ₁ < 0) × P(θ₂ > 0) where P(θᵢ > 0) = 1 - Φ(0; zᵢ, SEᵢ) and Φ is the standard normal CDF. High DCS indicates effects point in opposite directions with high probability—a fundamental disagreement about sign, not merely magnitude. **Uncertainty Quantification**: We bootstrap 1,000 resamples, drawing effect sizes from N(z, SE) for each study, computing DCS distributions, and extracting 95% percentile intervals. This provides per-study uncertainty bounds without Bayesian machinery. **Performance Evaluation**: Using binary replication outcomes as ground truth, we construct ROC curves and identify optimal classification thresholds via Youden's J statistic (maximizing TPR - FPR). **Statistical Validation**: Permutation tests (1,000 iterations) confirm DCS discriminates replication failure from success beyond chance. **Results Summary**: - Mean DCS: 0.384 (SD = 0.231) - Optimal threshold: 0.407 - At optimal threshold: Sensitivity = 0.71, Specificity = 0.73, Accuracy = 0.72 - ROC AUC: 0.78 - Permutation test: p < 0.001 These numbers establish that automated conflict detection works now. The scenarios explore what happens when it deploys. ### 2.3 Scenario Architecture Each scenario follows identical structure: **1. Triggering Conditions (2025-2026)**: 3-5 concrete, observable events that initiate the trajectory. These are not inevitable but represent strategically significant possibilities given current trends. **2. First-Order Effects (2026-2027)**: Immediate institutional and behavioral responses. What changes when validation becomes automated? **3. Second-Order Effects (2027-2028)**: Cascading consequences as researchers, institutions, and systems adapt. How does behavior change in response to changed incentives? **4. Third-Order Effects (2028-2029)**: Stabilized patterns and emergent structures. What becomes the new normal? **5. Phenomenological Immersion**: Throughout each scenario, we embed lived-experience vignettes—the day-in-the-life moments that reveal how abstract policy becomes visceral reality. **6. Analytical Extraction**: After immersion, we formalize the mechanisms, identify leverage points, and surface testable propositions. ### 2.4 Causal Discipline Every claim in the immersive sections traces back to defined triggering conditions through logical chains. We mark assumptions explicitly. We acknowledge where evidence thins. We distinguish what we know (DCS achieves 72% accuracy on RPP) from what we infer (how researcher

records.title: Research That Matters: A Call for Enhancing Rigour and Relevance in Artificial Intelligence Research in Endodontics
records.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is emerging as a powerful tool in dentistry, where endodontics can benefit significantly from its potential applications. From enhanced diagnostic accuracy to treatment planning and decision-making, optimisation, and outcome prediction, AI may significantly improve the clinical practice and the teaching of endodontics (Mohammad-Rahimi et al. 2024; Ourang et al. 2024). However, this still remains a largely unfulfilled promise, because many studies suffer from significant limitations or methodological flaws. Several factors contribute to this condition. First, as often seen with the advent of novel technology, there is a lack of scientific expertise in AI methodology by editors and reviewers, which may result in the eventual publication of studies that display limitations or, sometimes, even fundamental flaws in design, implementation, or validation. Conversely, technical publications may present sophisticated algorithms that solve problems with limited clinical utility or fail to address the nuanced challenges of real-world endodontic practice, mainly due to a lack of endodontic domain experts who could bridge the gap between AI engineers and the field of endodontics. Consequently, literature becomes populated with low-quality studies with oversold conclusions, but no conceivable clinical applicability. In this paper, the authors critically present the common pitfalls observed in current AI research in dentistry, and more specifically, in endodontics and then offer practical solutions to address these pitfalls in future research. The goal is to provide constructive guidance that can help establish rigorous standards for a field that is transitioning from research to real-life application. While we aim to present ideal scenarios that highlight these challenges, it is essential to acknowledge that every research study has limitations and shortcomings. These observations are not a critique of the researchers' intent but a call for consideration of these factors to enhance future work in the field. Foundational research has been conducted, and basic AI applications have been developed for endodontic applications. The next steps in endodontic AI research will have to address clinical translation and relevance which may often have been overlooked. This pitfall includes two interconnected challenges, but in distinct ways: developing AI models that solve problems of limited clinical significance and conducting studies under conditions that cannot translate to the real world. Some AI studies focus on tasks that, while technically interesting, have limited practical value in endodontic practice. Thus, the fundamental question researchers must ask is: Does this AI application solve a problem that clinicians face in daily practice, and would its solution meaningfully improve patient care or clinical workflow? Without this foundation, even technically sophisticated and highly performant models may risk being solutions in search of problems. Another core problem in AI studies is using non-representative training datasets. Some studies developed AI models under idealised or artificial conditions and then reported results as if they were clinically meaningful. This gap between experimental success and clinical utility may lead to a false sense of success. It impairs translation to practice, as models that perform well in controlled settings can fail or mislead in real clinical settings (Ibrahim et al. 2021). For example, there are AI models developed on ex vivo samples, phantom images, or synthetic entities (e.g., artificial lesions or artificial root cracks) that simplify the task. Training and testing an AI model on the detection of artificial root cracks in radiographic images of extracted teeth does not imply that the model can detect vertical root fractures in radiographic images of real patients. While convenient for initial experimentation, like pilot or proof-of-concept studies, such data lack the complexity and variable features of in vivo conditions. However, problems arise when researchers overinterpret their results or fail to acknowledge the fundamental limitations. Since these models often overestimate the capabilities of AI, we recommend that researchers test and validate their models on real clinical samples to verify their performance. Specifically, CONSORT-AI, a guideline for reporting AI clinical trials, explicitly noted that AI interventions should be evaluated in their intended clinical setting with patient-centric outcomes, not just technical metrics (Liu et al. 2020). Moreover, the American Dental Association (ADA) standard for dental AI validation (ANSI/ADA 1110-1) emphasises that AI radiology products must be tested on data that accurately represent the intended clinical cohort (2025). The validity of a supervised learning artificial intelligence system in endodontics is ultimately based on the reliability of its annotations. Labels provide the ground truth that supervised models rely on during training and evaluation. If the labels are poorly defined or inconsistently applied, that flawed representation of the dataset embeds itself into the model and can limit its performance. A frequent shortcoming is the reliance on a single annotator, with a lack of reporting on consensus or assessment of intra- or inter-rater reliability. Without such measures, the degree of subjectivity inherent in identifying features such as periapical radiolucencies or resorptive defects cannot be quantified. Even with measuring agreement, dentists only show moderate agreement with tasks such as caries identification on radiographs. These cases make establishing reliable reference annotations difficult (Devlin et al. 2021). Multiple annotations with experts who have differing judgements create fuzzy labels that can bias AI models if combined through simple majority voting (Zheng et al. 2021). Deep learning models are highly sensitive to noisy labels, and their performance drops as label noise increases (Karimi et al. 2020). There are especially strong effects when errors occur in minority classes with fewer examples, such as odontogenic tumours. Training with multiple annotators exposes inconsistency. The same image often receives conflicting labels, which shows that disagreement is not random but systematically influenced by lesion subtlety, annotator experience, and bias (Büttner et al. 2023). Probabilistic aggregation methods such as multi-annotator competence estimation (MACE) and the Dawid–Skene method better estimate true labels by modelling annotator reliability and bias compared to simple consensus (Venanzi et al. 2014). A recent study that tested various annotation aggregation strategies found that MACE worked best for single-modality datasets (e.g., radiographs), while Dawid–Skene excelled in multimodal combined datasets (e.g., images and text) (Klein et al. 2025). This highlights the importance of structured training and calibration of annotators before starting large-scale labelling. Another recurring weakness lies in the absence of detailed annotation protocols. When definitions of pathological findings, outcome measures, or anatomical boundaries are vague, annotators may apply inconsistent criteria, producing noisy labels that are very variable, heterogeneous, and difficult to replicate. AI papers often fail to describe how ambiguous cases, such as faint bone discontinuities or borderline artefact lines, were handled. This is particularly troubling in endodontics, where anatomical structures such as root apices, the location of apical foramina, and canal boundaries are subtle and sometimes difficult to accurately define. Similar concerns have been raised in reviews of dental AI research, which emphasise the importance of transparent and standardised annotation methods to ensure reproducibility and clinical trustworthiness (Schwendicke et al. 2021; Uribe et al. 2025). The problem becomes even more complicated when the expertise and calibration of annotators are not reported. This causes uncertainty as to whether images were assessed by highly trained specialists, junior clinicians, residents or students. Finally, the data source is often under-documented. This refers to systematic documentation of how data, especially imaging data, were acquired and processed, including scanner/imaging machine specifications, exposure settings, or artefact prevalence are rarely described in detail. Each of these factors may influence the appearance of endodontic features and thereby bias the annotations (Norgeot et al. 2020; Liu et al. 2020). The cumulative effect of these deficiencies constrains the achievable accuracy of the model and lowers confidence in its clinical applicability. Recent standards, such as International Organisation for Standardisation (ISO) 18374:2025 (2025), the first international standard specifically governing AI in dentistry, provides requirements for data generation, annotation, and processing in AI-based dental radiograph analysis to enhance reproducibility and trustworthiness. Moreover, the ADA standard for dental AI (ANSI/ADA 1110-1) underscores that annotation should follow standardised definitions and record metadata about the annotator experience (2025). Even though some studies don't adopt this standard, its existence signals the community's recognition that annotation is a first-order problem that needs to be addressed. Future directions include smarter label aggregation, semi-supervised learning, and reference modalities (e.g., micro-CT) to improve annotation quality and reduce human inconsistency (Klein et al. 2025). Various studies have tried to suggest new models specific to endodontic tasks. However, they do not benchmark and compare the “novel” method against state-of-the-art models. Without comprehensive comparisons, there is a possibility of presenting new, complex models as superior when simpler or more established approaches might yield similar results. This may mislead the scientific community, as these models may be prematurely adopted despite offering little or no real improvement, ultimately hindering scientific progress (Isensee et al. 2024). Similarly, Bassi et al. (2024) suggested that “unfair comparisons” are one of the challenges in studies to propose a new AI model, which leads to biases and should be treated cautiously in real-world situations. Additionally, some studies introduced minor tweaks as major innovations (e.g., swapping out a model component for another well-established one or applying a simple post-processing step), and prioritise algorithmic sophistication over practical applicability. This practice may mislead and promote a culture of exaggerated claims and false novelty under the guise of advanced AI development. For example, Schneider et al. (2022) showed that more complex models did not necessarily correlate with better performance in their teeth segmentation benchmarking study. In the 3D medical image segmentation task, Isensee et al. (2024) demonstrated in their benchmarking study in 2024 that their original model, introduced in 2021 (Isensee et al. 2021), still outperformed many more recently popularised models in the field. The authors suggested that there was a bias toward new AI architectures, which indicates a need for stricter validation standards. Moreover, when comparative models are applied to clinical tasks, the selection often appears arbitrary (Schneider et al. 2022). Various studies reported unfavourable outcomes for comparative models, while using slightly modified models (such as architecture, learning pipelines, and initialisation), better outcomes could be achieved. The significance of these limitations is the potential to underestimate the true capabilities of AI models. For instance, some studies may report that humans outperform AI in specific tasks based on comparisons with a single, potentially suboptimal model configuration. However, without systematic ablation studies to explore alternative architectures, hyperparameters, or training strategies, such conclusions may underestimate AI's true capabilities. Therefore, a systematic, comprehensive, and “hypothesis-driven” approach for the selection of AI models and their configurations was suggested (Schneider et al. 2022; Schwendicke et al. 2021). The reasons for choosing the selected approach or model should be justified (Weikert et al. 2021). In general, the selection of AI model types should be driven by factors including, but not limited to, the dataset size and distribution, complexity of the task, interpretability, and computational and validation costs (De Hond et al. 2022). Another critical challenge in model development is the claim that AI models are explainable because of post hoc visualisation tools such as saliency maps. While these techniques can offer insights into model decision-making, they do not achieve true explainability by design. True explainability requires that the model architecture or learning process inherently produces interpretable outputs or structured reasoning, rather than relying on post hoc processing (Rudin 2019). Overstating the level of explainability can be misleading to reviewers and end-users and compromise trust. Beyond data preparation, the credibility of endodontic AI research rests on the strength of its validation and analysis. A recurring methodological weakness is the practice of reporting a single result from a single model run without accounting for natural variation in sample data. Such single-point estimates risk overstating the model's capability. It is common for studies to report apparently impressive performance metrics such as accuracies exceeding 95%. Such results may be misleading if derived from a single validation set. To mitigate this instability, more rigorous approaches such as cross-validation should be employed (Bradshaw et al. 2023). This ensures that each case contributes to both training and testing, which provides a distribution of performance estimates rather than a single point value, and reduces the risk that results are driven by a favourable split. When cross-validation results are reported, it is often unclear which model is ultimately presented in the publication. In many cases, authors appear to have selected the “best” fold based on validation performance. This information is not always clearly stated and could lead to a misrepresentation of the cross-validation process. The lack of transparency of the cross-validation process further introduces the possibility of the lack of true testing on an unseen dataset. This necessitates the need for test data to be split from the dataset (i.e., held-out test set) before cross-validation is carried out. Inappropriate data partitioning is common, with images or slices from the same patient appearing in both training and test sets. In endodontic imaging, a scenario could arise where cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) volumes from a single patient are divided into multiple slices and then distributed across both training and test sets. This is called ‘data leakage’ and can inflate the model's performance by allowing it to memorise patient-specific feature patterns rather than learn generalisable features (Apicella et al. 2025). Such practices result in overfitting, which may yield deceptively high-performance reporting, despite notable reductions in performance when the model is tested on new, unseen patient data or images (Aliferis and Simon 2024).
