records.title: Creating the Ideal Posthuman Body? Cyborg Sex and Gender in the Work of Buzzati, Vacca, and Ammaniti
records.abstract: In recent years much critical attention has been focused on the figure of the cyborg or cybernetic organism: a hybrid being that evolves where the boundaries between human and machine are open to transgression.1 Yet despite its implicit promise of an “enhanced” physique and superior reasoning abilities, to what extent can (or should) we consider this figure as radical, subversive and innovative? In an Italian context, researchers such as Antonio Caronia have theorized posthuman or cyborg phenomena for an Italophone readership, chronicling their development across the centuries and mapping their multifaceted morphologies as central figures of science fiction. However, as is the case with another recent Italian publication on this topic (Vincenzo Tagliasco's Dizionario degli esseri umani fantastici e artificiali) Caronia's attention is directed beyond Italy, to Anglophone—and in particular North American—cultural production. Consequently, both texts markedly privilege Anglophone literature, film and criticism to the exclusion of Italian discourses and cultural artefacts.2 The work of Giuseppe O. Longo (Il nuovo Golem and Homo technologicus) also offers a theoretical engagement with the relationship between humans and technology, but the only Italian literary texts to which significant reference is made are Longo's own. In contrast, this article endeavors to redirect critical attention onto other Italian sources, in an initial attempt to identify and analyse aspects of Italian engagements with the cyborg and bring them into dialogue with Anglophone theoretical work.From the anxieties about mechanised men and women in Massimo Bontempelli's Minnie la candida (1927), to Primo Levi's probing of the golem myth in “Il servo,” twentieth-century Italian literature offers a Rich, if underexplored, array of cyborg characters which both echo those to be found in Anglophone texts and can be been seen to embody and exemplify concerns emanating from a specifically Italian cultural context. Focusing on cyborg figures in three texts—Dino Buzzati's Il grande ritratto (1960), Roberto Vacca's Il robot e il computer (1963), and Niccolò Ammaniti's short story “Ferro” (1996)—this article identifies and analyses approaches to a series of sex/gender issues and attempts to trace the positions assumed by the authors in question back to earlier influential works. More specifically, I question the degree to which these works can be read as encouraging progressive rather than normative attitudes. I argue that despite purporting to convey futuristic innovation that challenges conventional notions of gender roles and identity, these narratives show the influence of problematic ideologies proposed by late nineteenth- and early twentieth-century figures such as the Futurists and the criminologist Cesare Lombroso—writers whose work provides a sometimes disturbingly relevant point of reference for this article. Thus the texts analysed allow us to trace the shadows of key Italian thinkers in works that might more readily be seen as linked to Anglophone traditions of science fiction.This article investigates a number of interrelated issues: the ways in which cyborg narratives portray sexual dynamics between cyborgs and “non-enhanced” humans; the erotic charge of fusion with technology; how such narratives engage with mind/body dualism; the ways in which dominant understandings of gender roles and sexed bodies are insistently replicated through fictional accounts of cyborg bodies; representations of male desire for creative power. I have chosen the texts under consideration because they allow me to compare diachronically a series of male perspectives on the sexing, gendering, and eroticization of both male and female cyborgs, sexual interaction with cyborg figures and narrative dramatisations of both the mind/body split and fusion with technology. The reference to “cyborg sex” in my title is meant to indicate both sexed bodies and sex with cyborgs. Unlike “cyber sex” that involves the willful shrugging off of gender, sex and sexual orientation since the vast majority of individuals who enter the virtual dimension of MUDS—Multi-User Domains—do so under an assumed identity (see Anne Scott Sørensen), representations of “cyborg sex” often strive to reinforce or replicate more normative human practices. A key question here is why this might be so in an Italian context; why do even recent texts resonate so strongly with the supplanted authority of Lombroso, for example?As a guide to subsequent observations, and in an effort to further contextualize my remarks in relation to existing and ongoing intellectual debate, I preface my considerations of the selected texts with a brief outline of the approaches to sex, gender, and the erotics of technology that inform this article.My principal concern is our often erotically charged relationship with technology, especially in relation to sexual dynamics between biological human and cyborg beings. I explore the sexual draw of machines whose status hovers on the shifting boundaries that psychoanalysis has drawn between conscious and unconscious, ego and id, and which inhabit the unheimlich overlap of self and other. Many of the sexed and gendered tensions that mark more contemporary conceptions of libidinal relationships with technology are clearly evident in the writings of the Futurists. For example, besides bombastically celebrating the “bellezza nuova” and speed of motor vehicles, Marinetti describes the loving care with which a train driver washes “il gran corpo possente della sua locomotiva” with “le tenerezze minuziose e sapienti di un amante che accarezzi la sua donna adorata.”3 Arnaldo Ginna similarly confuses the anthropomorphization of the car as a phallic extension of its male driver with the sexualization of the car as a female vessel. In the same paragraph he writes that the car has become the necessary prolongation of the worker's sensations, but that the car may soon be the only lover we desire (qtd. in Verdone 91). records.title: Florence Kelley: Pragmatist, Feminist, Socialist
records.abstract: supreme court justice felix frankfurter said in 1953 that Florence Kelley “had probably the largest single share in shaping the social history of the United States during the first 30 years of the 20th Century” (Frankfurter x). Kelley is an unusual figure to discuss in a philosophical journal, perhaps because she has generally been classified only as a social scientist. Yet, as I discovered, she is a wonderful thinking partner, sometimes raising more philosophical questions than she resolves. Her commitments, struggles, failures, and accomplishments problematize and reveal new insights into pragmatist pluralism, feminist political choices, and the role of socialism in early pragmatism. Bringing her into the feminist pragmatist discussion gives us more examples of how to approach problem-solving from feminist and pragmatist perspectives.1Florence Kelley and Jane Addams first met when Kelley knocked on Hull House's door early one snowy December morning in 1891. She was fleeing with her three small children from her physically abusive husband in New York, needing an occupation and a home in Chicago. She became the only early resident who was a single mother. Kelley spent most of the next decade at Hull House. Kelley and Addams had similar family backgrounds and became close friends, although they had dramatically different personalities. One thing they shared in common was that both were very close to their politician fathers.Kelley's father was a longtime progressive congressman from Pennsylvania. He helped to develop her social consciousness by taking her along on his investigations of industrial conditions when, as a child herself, she often saw the horrifying conditions of children's work environments. At two in the morning, she witnessed the “terrifying sight” of boys younger than herself working near the steel mills’ red-hot furnaces and molten metal. With her father, she also witnessed young boys called “dogs” working in glass factories. Each glass blower was assisted by one of these boys who knelt with his head near the oven as the glass came out from the furnaces to prepare the hot mold for the blower's next project. These events left her with the “astonished impression of the utter unimportance of children compared with products” (Kelley, “My Philadelphia” 56–57).She entered Cornell University at age 16 and was drawn to the study of social science and economics. Like many college-bound young women in the late nineteenth century, she quickly became committed to social reform, focusing on women and children's social and economic conditions. As Kelley said in 1882, in her first published article after college, “In the field of sociology, there is brainwork waiting for women which men cannot do” (“Need Our Working Women” 521). In their lives and studies, young college women like Kelley experienced the inequalities and suffering around them and were looking for a solution. Kelley developed an approach that focused on both the causes as well as the effects of the social problems she worked to eradicate. She believed that college-educated women and working-class women could work together to produce knowledge and change.Kelley was exposed briefly to Marxism and socialism in her college years when a family friend convalesced in their home. This man's father had known Karl Marx, and he shared some Marxist pamphlets with Kelley (Autobiography 72). After college, when she continued her studies in Zurich, she became immersed in Marxism. She returned to the United States three years later, with her Russian Marxist husband and their three children. She expected to continue her Marxist work with the New York Socialist Labor Party, but the party expelled her and her husband. She then turned her attention to researching working women's financial and social struggles.In Chicago, Kelley's early research into local living and working conditions was published in the ground-breaking Hull House Maps and Papers, written by Hull House residents (Addams et al.), considered a pioneering work in sociology and an early example of what became cultural geography. Her investigations into child labor, sweatshops, and industrial conditions led to her position as Illinois's first chief factory inspector. Armed with data and the support of the Hull House network, she successfully lobbied the Illinois legislature for laws protecting industrial workers. She drafted proposed legislation, and when legislation was passed, she and her team of inspectors enforced the new regulations.After leaving Hull House in 1899, she became the first head of the National Consumers League (NCL), where she continued to change working conditions by shaping consumers’ choices. Under Kelley's leadership, the NCL became “the single most successful lobbying agency on behalf of legislative protections for working women and children”(Sklar, “Hull House Maps” 138). Kelley and Henry Street Settlement founder Lillian Wald also originated the innovative and powerful federal Children's Bureau. Her activism and her mentoring of other political leaders helped lay the foundations for the 1930s New Deal legislation. American democratic culture was altered by Kelley's continuing work to modify capitalism's brutalities and establish legal safeguards for workers, particularly for women and children.In her work in Chicago, Kelley became a pragmatist, influenced by her work with Addams and the philosophers and social scientists in Chicago. In claiming that Kelley is a pragmatist, I'm not claiming that she is a philosopher in any traditional sense. She approached all public problems as one trained in the social sciences, but then, as in current times, pragmatism was and is one of the philosophies and methodologies that support the social sciences (Morgan; Biesta) and many emerging fields.2 As an interdisciplinary field, early pragmatism stood at the boundaries of multiple disciplines. Pragmatism and the early social sciences in the United States developed in the same intellectual and social milieu. Pragmatist philosophers, particularly Addams, Dewey, James, and Mead, were instrumental in the early evolution of the social sciences.3 Addams's stature as a foundational figure in sociology, social work, and peace work had traditionally placed her in the social sciences. Kelley was also a participant in the evolution of the social sciences.Since its founding, the social science fields were split between those who advocated the perspective of the disinterested observer and those who were immersed in social reform. Women tended to fill the latter ranks—the practitioners who theorized from personal experiences. Kelley took the approach to social science more often practiced by women, combining her work for reform with her investigations.4 She was interested in the particulars of the situation rather than a generalized theoretical approach.The first decade of Hull House was also the first decade of the new all-male sociology department at the University of Chicago. Although many of the sociologists were involved in Hull House, Addams rejected their concept of a settlement house as a laboratory where the workers become “experts” (Deegan 35). In her criticism of the “sociological laboratory,” Addams said that settlements should be “more human and spontaneous” (Addams, Twenty Years 178). Settlements placed the individual needs of the people in the community before theory-building.5 In a letter to University of Chicago president Harper, Addams said that the Hull House residents were “living in the 19th ward, not as students, but as citizens” (qtd. in Deegan 38).The early divisions in the developing fields of the social sciences are often portrayed as gendered, with women's social science (like that of Addams) more frequently engaged in and growing out of applied community work and advocacy. In contrast, most male social scientists wanted to take a distanced observer perspective (Muncy 43–45; Sklar, “Hull House Maps” 114–15; Rynbrandt 44–54). Another way to look at this divide is to consider it a pragmatist vs. non-pragmatist perspective in the social sciences. The early social sciences appealed to many women reformers because they contained the same aspects that we would consider pragmatist: local, particularized knowledge, experiential engagement, and efforts to improve social conditions.6 Kelley was committed to empirical research, but, like her Hull House colleagues, she expected that her research would result in social change, not in new theories.Pragmatist methodology relies on “situated creativity” (Colapietro 1), which begins with lived experience, localized social context, and shared reflection. Pragmatist thinking and theorizing start with the particular lived situation and return to those situations, or as James said, “[i]t begins with concreteness, and returns and ends with it” (934). The local community and historical context are starting points for thinking and the basis for final reflection, which depends on having, as Addams wrote in 1895, “an enthusiasm for the possibilities of locality” (Addams et al., Hull House Maps 207).As a theorist and a practitioner, Kelley used these concrete situations to find and then combat the causes of the evils she battled (Goldmark 67). Instead of ideals such as generalized human rights, Kelley focused on and engaged with particular settings, such as piecemeal work done in tenements, children working in industries, or the hours worked by women in factories. As she said in 1898: [I]f you are to speak as one having authority and not as the scribes in these matters of the common daily life and experience . . . you must suffer from the dirty streets, the universal ugliness, the lack of oxygen in the air you daily breathe, the endless struggle with soot and dust and insufficient water supply, the hanging from a strap on the overcrowded streetcar at the end of your day's work. (Kelley, “Hull House” 550)Like Addams and Dewey, Kelley was committed to social ethics that transcended individual ethics. She believed that changes in the law would promote equality and protect the space for social ethics through protections for social rights.7 Although human rights may appear to be individual personal rights, in Some Ethical Gains through Legislation, Kelley said asserting those rights “invariably brings the experience that they are historically interwoven with the rights of innumerable other people,” particularly “the weakest and most defenseless persons in the community” (229–30). She claims that social rights, like the right to childhood, the right to leisure, and suffrage for women, must happen through collective, not individual, action, which points to this the necessity of legislation. Social ethics requires thinking about the good of society and also requires a community to be involved in creating those goods.One reason to bring Kelley into a philosophical discussion of early pragmatism is to note how she influenced and was influenced by the pragmatist figures of her day. When Addams and Kelley first met, their philosophical orientations were dramatically different.8 In her first endeavors at Hull House, Addams had approached settlement work from the perspective of social intercourse around the humanities, consistent with her liberal arts education.9 After Kelley arrived, Addams and Hull House moved toward data-driven social science investigations and active support of the labor unions. Kelley's expertise in social science research, developed in her studies at Cornell and refined by later investigative work, added a systemic, class-based analysis to Hull House reform efforts, as evidenced in Hull House Maps and Papers (Addams et al.). That data became a tool of social change, particularly in Hull House's successful legislative work.10Kelley's commitment to race, class, and gender pluralism was evident throughout her work. She became deeply committed to fighting racial inequity, and in that work, she developed a relationship with Du Bois. After her death, Du Bois said that “save for Jane Addams, there is not another social worker in the United States who has had either her insight or her daring, so far as the American Negro is concerned” (131). Along with Addams, Dewey, and Du Bois, Kelley was a founding member of the NAACP. As an active member of its Board, she worked tirelessly on its committees, including those responsible for the budget and initiatives such as Federal Aid to Education, Anti-Lynching, and the Inequal Expenditure of School Funds. Her work for racial justice followed the same research-based methodology that she and Addams developed in their early years at Hull House. Du Bois described Kelley's approach: “Always, she asked questions: pointed, penetrating, devastating questions, and to these questions she wanted answers and was herself more than willing to furnish answers by work and inquiry and thought” (131). She analyzed upcoming legislative bills to determine their impact on discriminatory racial practices and did research to find data to support or critique forthcoming legislation. She was particularly concerned with equalizing funding for African American schools and vigorously opposed lynching. She lobbied Congress, gathered signatures, rallied her social reform colleagues, and drew on her connections within several national organizations to advocate for or against bills that affected racial equity. She didn't hesitate to engage in protests personally. In 1917, “she marched in the silent protest parade down the streets of New York to dramatize her opposition to the brutal savagery displayed by white authorities and citizens against Negroes in the East St. Louis, Illinois race riots of that year” (Athey 257).Kelley was raised in a family committed to women's suffrage, and her early exposure to the fight for women's rights contributed to her larger social justice perspective. Her great aunt Sarah Pugh was a well-known advocate for women's suffrage and African American rights and a friend of Lucretia Mott and Elizabeth Cady Stanton. Kelley's father was a friend of Susan B. Anthony, and he was an early sponsor of suffrage amendments in the House of Representatives. He regularly spoke on behalf of women's rights (Kelley, Autobiography 61; Sklar, Florence Kelley 46–48).Kelley's commitment to women's issues led to research and activism focused on women's working conditions and children in poverty, two threads of research that continued throughout her entire career. From her earliest studies at Cornell, women and children were her primary subjects. In her feminist economic commitment to working-class women, she constructed “a class analysis of contemporary society” often using “gender as a surrogate for class.” Even when she extended her work to include the conditions of all laborers, “her political-social-rhetorical base was female” (Sklar, “Hull House Maps” 116). In her later career, she became concerned about public health issues around infant mortality numbers and mothers dying in childbirth, which led to her work co-creating the federal Children's Bureau and her enthusiastic support of its programs.Kelley was vice president of the National American Woman Suffrage Association (NAWSA) for many years and actively worked for the suffrage cause. She joined the first National Woman's Party, which was more aggressive and militant in its suffrage work than the older suffrage leaders (Goldmark 180). The National Woman's Party (NWP) was disbanded when suffrage was achieved. A new organization with the same name was formed to fight for the Equal Rights Amendment, a constitutional amendment requiring the government to treat women the same as men, which touched off a debate within the National Woman's Party about the meaning of equality.After an emotionally and intellectually agonizing struggle, Kelley decided she could not support the ERA. In taking this move, Kelley became part of a feminist debate that engaged women throughout the twentieth century: Should feminists advocate for the “same” treatment as men or advocate for “equal” treatment, which considers women's differing gender needs?11 She did not believe that requiring women to be treated the same as men resulted in equality for women. records.title: Symposium Introduction: On Pragmatism's Potential for Making Futures in Troubled Times
records.abstract: Today, it seems that shared points of orientation are no longer available, and hence that the possibility of a clear and safe future is increasingly in jeopardy. Due to events related to climate change such as growing inequalities, mass migration, and the rise of populism, the question how to conceive of futures that are different from the ones that present themselves as obvious or necessary emerges as a pressing concern.1 In trying to understand our current predicament, Isabelle Stengers suggests that our epoch is marked by the intrusion of Gaia.2 This means that the Earth itself has claimed a seat at the negotiation table and that it cannot be neglected anymore in political debates about the future. This is not to say that the Earth would be an indulgent partner that gives in to the needs and demands of humankind. Rather, Stengers imagines Gaia as ticklish, not easy to satisfy, and ready to lash out unpredictably, which makes it extremely hard to imagine life on Earth in the near and far future.3 In the midst of this turmoil, education for sustainable development positions itself as a way out of the trouble. Sustainable development education does not suggest a straightforward or uniform pedagogical path but covers a variety of different approaches and methods. While the more instrumentalist take on education stresses the importance of instilling knowledge, skills, and competences to solve sustainability challenges, more emancipatory ideas criticize this problem-solving logic and emphasize fostering the critical and transformative capabilities of individual learners.4 What both courses of action seem to share, however, is a belief in the possibility of making an imagined future real and a belief that education is the preferred and most efficacious route to that future. In doing so, these initiatives provide a certain sense of orientation, respectively toward problem-solving pedagogies and critical-transformative teaching. In providing these points of orientation, education for sustainable development seems to reframe education in a cruelly optimistic way by making us long for an impossible future.5 What is at stake in the issue of thinking about education in light of the intrusion of Gaia is, however, maybe not so much to try and stabilize a troubled future, i.e., to overcome a crisis, but to find ways of staying with the trouble.6 Interestingly, recent years have seen a renewed attention in pragmatism as a way to navigate the tumultuous waters between cruelly optimistic and tragically defeatist conceptions of education for sustainable development.7 The aim of this symposium is therefore to reflect on the ways in which pragmatic ideas might help to deal with the pressing contemporary demand that is perhaps too often formulated in terms of “sustainable development,” namely how to inherit a world marked by socio-ecological destruction and pass it on to a next generation. This is a thoroughly educational challenge that touches upon many discussions within philosophy and theory of education. All too often, pragmatism has been deployed in educational discussions in terms of problem-solving pedagogies, or experience-oriented education. However, this symposium puts forward an alternative idea of pragmatism as as the art of the possible, as having the potential to make thought creative of a different future.8 Returning to pragmatism cannot be done without at the same time problematizing some of the ideas that are central to pragmatism, traditionally conceived. The point of departure of the symposium is that these pragmatist ideas cannot just be “applied” to a new situation, but that they — in a truly pragmatic sense — need to be refashioned in light of the demands put by a new indeterminate situation. More in particular and against the background of the cruel optimism of sustainability education, we take issue with the specific “melioristic” mindset that undergirds many pragmatist texts. This melioristic mindset coincides with the progressive-optimistic belief that social problems can be solved through educational intervention and that, in doing so, the future can be safeguarded.9 This kind of modern belief in progress is nowadays being put to the test by the intrusion of Gaia. However, dealing with this new predicament also constitutes an opportunity to reread pragmatism differently. Rereading does not signify an uncritical return to tradition to find answers to issues of the present. Neither does it mean to put away this tradition in light of the critique and criticism that has debunked or denounced it. Rather, it means to engage with these texts in a postcritical or affirmative way, which means that one tries to draw out a difference that might produce a slight shift in the meaning of a text and make it come to matter in a new and unforeseen way.10 In recent years, the works of classical authors that have been more peripheral in the reception of pragmatism in educational theory (such as William James or Alfred North Whitehead) have proven very helpful in rereading pragmatism and opening up new directions. At the same time, contemporary new materialist authors such as Donna Haraway and Isabelle Stengers have afforded possibilities for rereading pragmatist thinking as well.11 Again, rereading does not just entail a refurbishment of an old text in light of criticism; it is most of all also a rewriting of sources of the past according to a new sense of orientation (or a loss thereof) that belongs to the present. More in particular, the contributors to the symposium pursue four transitions in rereading early pragmatic texts. The first transition takes issue with the naturalistic experimentalism that haunts much of John Dewey's thought on science, but also his ideas about democracy and community. Although Dewey rejects a one-sided focus on science as a purely cognitivist endeavor and the sole road to knowledge, in favor of a more integrated project of inquiry that includes social dimensions as well, he still adheres to a particular modern idea of scientific rationality.12 In other words, Dewey criticizes the scientistic position, resituates knowledge production from “the head” to the transactions between organism and environment, and democratizes the scientific method. At the same time, however, he leaves the scientific method based on incrementalism and rational communication unchallenged. At this point, rereadings of James have been helpful in transitioning from Dewey's experimental naturalism to a cosmological pluralism that works experimentally to cultivate an ongoing and unfinished pluriverse, diverging with itself all the way down to problematize the convergence by communication pursued by Dewey.13 A second transition attempts a rereading of pragmatism that destabilizes the humanist foundations on which much pragmatist thinking is built, and which has set the stage for the reception of pragmatism in educational theory. Although Dewey's thought is grounded within a Darwinist worldview that stresses embeddedness within an environment and contingent transformation, it has often been read as centered around concerns about democracy and education understood in a humanist way. To a certain extent, this humanist orientation has been radicalized in Richard Rorty's grafting of pragmatism onto the linguistic turn which shifted the scope of pragmatism from experience — a still rather broad and not necessarily humanist category — to language, the prerogative of human beings.14 In dehumanizing pragmatism and recasting it as a thoroughly posthumanist philosophy, Alfred North Whitehead's work aims to undo the bifurcation of humans and nature, and suggests a process ontology of actual occasions that prehends human and other-than-human beings alike.15 A third transition concerns the affectivity or mood of pragmatist theorizing. More in particular, several of the contributions here question the optimism that seems to underlie many pragmatist ideas, namely the belief that problems can be solved by applying a specific “can do” attitude to them. This optimism can be criticized for being naïve, overconfident, or downright cruel, especially in light of the problematic situations that have come in the wake of the intrusion of Gaia.16 However, this does not mean to abandon all hope and give in to cynicism, fatalism, or pessimism. Rather, what emerges is the thoroughly tragic sense of all educational endeavors, which refers to a larger awareness of the impediments to success, the prospects for failure, and the limits to our effort.17 Embracing this tragic sense requires us to abandon the belief in a transcendence that saves — be it God or Science — and to take seriously the uncertainty that looms in every educational act. It is a more complex sentiment that forces us to learn to dwell in uncertainty, instead of trying to overcome it. The last transition pursued here has to do with the image of pragmatism as a very particular American philosophy that is inextricably linked with the history of the United States during the Progressive Era. This reading situates the development of pragmatism amidst tensions particular to the national context of the United States, such as a lack of deep roots that coincides with a sense of perpetual self-invention; an optimistic belief in science, progress, and meritocracy; and a struggle to combine a common national identity with the plurality of various communities.18 Instead, the contributions to this symposium point our attention toward the many exchanges between intellectual traditions, both today and in the past, that have sought to articulate a philosophy of difference and that have found inspiration in the writings of James, Whitehead, and other pragmatists.19 In that sense, the last transition attempts to move away from the “American exceptionalism” of pragmatism towards a version of pragmatism as a situated and terrestrial philosophy of plural worlds in the making, as can be found in the writings of Isabelle Stengers, Bruno Latour, and Donna Haraway. It is this last tension that is taken up immediately in the first contribution. The first article provides philosophical reflections on the development of pragmatism as an intellectual current. Relying on an image of generations, Lynda Stone describes pragmatism as a multifarious philosophical current that includes a diversity of approaches, fields, and concepts, and that is marked by a few generational divides that have crystallized over time. She delves into the tensions between pragmatism as an American philosophy, or even “the” American philosophy, on the one hand, and the variety of interpretations of pragmatism from an international audience, on the other hand. In relation to the issue of democracy, which is a recurring topic throughout her contribution, Stone problematizes the American exceptionalism of pragmatism. Her text is a philosophical introduction to pragmatist thought covering three generations that each gave rise to a different conception of the question of democracy. She sketches the longue durée of pragmatist philosophy and gives insight into the historical background against which the contributions that follow are written. With Stefano Oliverio's article, we arrive in the New Climatic Regime. Building on the work of Michel Serres and Bruno Latour, his contribution shows how the intrusion of Gaia has brought the Modern Constitution to failure. The Modern Constitution is predicated on the split between Nature and Culture which haunts several of the dualisms that have structured philosophical ideas and theories (active versus passive, subject versus object, social versus material). Giving insight into the reconfiguring of life on Earth after the intrusion of Gaia, Oliverio rereads Dewey's idea of educability through several of the lenses offered by Latour. He proposes to shift the focus from mind as a modern substance and prerogative of the human being, to minding as a verb, an act of taking care in which a certain sense of attentiveness is being realized that gives way to a pragmatic art of consequences as opposed to the prevailing sense of negligence. In doing so, he reimagines the school as a site of collective inquiry. The idea of collective inquiry is taken up further in Hans Schildermans's contribution on problematization. In this article, Dewey's writings on problematic situations and the processes of inquiry they might give rise to are taken as a point of departure to reconsider the nature of knowledge production in the Anthropocene. Rereading Dewey's ideas on inquiry alongside Isabelle Stengers's work on problematization and Stuart Kauffman's biology of enabling constraints, Schildermans suggests study as a practice of giving a problematic situation the power to transform our ways of thinking and feeling, thereby opening up the future anew. Rather than being entailed by laws of probability and predictability, the future comes forward as a plurality of possibilities enabled in confrontation with the constraints posed by the problematic situation. Such problematic situations and their problematizations do not so much require particular problem-solving pedagogies, but rather a pragmatics of a world to-be-made in which every response signifies a new mode of inhabiting that world. The question what it means to think in the course of such processes of inquiry or practices of study takes center stage in the article by Joris Vlieghe. Rereading Dewey's reflections on thinking as set out in his book How We Think?, together with Giorgio Agamben's writing on (im)potentiality, he tries to remediate the proceduralism and conservatism that is lurking in Dewey's account of thinking. Vlieghe foregrounds thinking as an experience of anonymity, rupture, possibility, and community that cannot be privatized and that emerges when our habitual ways of living our lives are halted or rendered inoperative. Therefore, he argues that thinking is not merely a theoretical or mental pursuit, but that it is a matter of life or, in Agamben's phrasing, that it coincides with a form-of-life in which life cannot be segregated from its form. It is this existential dimension of thought that relates to the educational quality of potentiality as impotentiality, which holds the possibility for true transformation. Post-truth as our contemporary social and political predicament constitutes the point of departure of Bianca Thoilliez's contribution. She argues that the post-truth world is a particular effect of the combination of epistemological paranoia and widespread distrust in political institutions. The post-truth world comes with particular challenges for education as well. Rereading Peircean fallibilism and Jamesian pluralism alongside Haraway's situated knowledges and Latour's down-to-earth politics, she suggests alliances of inquiry and cultural provisioning as possible educational responses to the post-truth world. Thoilliez grounds her propositions via excerpts from the novel My Family and Other Animals by Gerald Durrell. This amounts to a pedagogy that does not try to fix or evade problems, but that creates the circumstances to stay with them. The circumstances created by this down-to-earth pedagogy aim to restore the mutual trust and common ground necessary for exploring life in common together. It is in taking care of truths in a post-truth world, in a thoroughly fallibilistic and pluralistic fashion, that education becomes possible again. In the contribution that follows, Martin Savranksy argues for a slight shift in perspective on the question of life in common. Drawing inspiration from the ancient practical and spiritual arts of living, he raises awareness for the interdependencies between philosophy, education, and questions of living and dying on a fragile Earth. Savransky rereads James's writings in connection with the spiritual exercises of Ancient Greek philosophical schools as described by Pierre Hadot to reconsider a philosophical life as being lived in the hold of the possibility of learning to think and live differently. Disentangling dimensions of orality and sociality present in the ancient art of living, he elaborates the idea of philosophy as an apprenticeship in living and dying, in which the values of life and death themselves are being revaluated in light of an ideal mode of living that relies on a specific educational practice — the spiritual exercise — to realize itself. In that sense, he refashions pragmatism as an immanent experiment with the possibility of engendering new ways of inhabiting the Earth. The final paper of this special issue explicitly problematizes the optimism that undergirds much pragmatist theorizing. Petra Mikulan takes issue with the ethics of salvation that tries to remediate the so-called externalities of the Anthropocene, because such redemptionist ethics is bound up with particular Western colonial logics of appropriation, extraction, and exploitation of human, social, and natural resources. She is inspired by current initiatives by students such as Climate Strike and Fridays for Future that enact walking out of the social institution of formal education, and she reflects upon questions of subjectivity and positionality in her own teaching practice. Mikulan rereads the social philosophies of Dewey and Jane Addams through the lens of Stengers's speculative pragmatism to articulate an ethics of refusal. Such an ethics of refusal draws attention to the thoroughly educational problem underlying formal education in light of the Anthropocene, namely how to prepare the younger generation for a future that is not properly ours. Rereading classical pragmatist texts in conjunction with contemporary authors and situated by the intrusion of Gaia, opens up a possibility for renewal in which the pragmatist habit of thought appears as a way of taking care of the consequences of our ideas. In that sense, it is an art of the possible that embraces thought as an adventure bound by a world that is never given, but is always in the making. It is in the attempt to think with this world — and not against it in name of whatever foundation — that all certainties, categories, and principles start to tremble and that a possibility for genuine experimentation is opened up, in which futures radically different from the ones that are probable can start to reshape our ways of thinking and feeling. In this, and situated by the trouble caused by the intrusion of Gaia, pragmatism comes forward as an adventure of hope that contains a potential for making futures in troubled times. HANS SCHILDERMANS is a Postdoctoral Researcher in the Department of Education at the University of Vienna; e-mail <[email protected]>. His primary areas of scholarship are the history and theory of higher education, critical university studies, epistemologies of educational research, and contemporary pragmatist philosophies of education. He is the author of Experiments in Decolonizing the University: Towards an Ecology of Study (Bloomsbury, 2021).

records.title: Psychology in Edgar Allan Poe
records.abstract: From the advent of psychology and psychoanalysis, founders and proponents of these academic disciplines have shown interest in both Poe's creative genius and his fictional works. As a case in point, in his early psychoanalytic study of the figure of the double, The Double: A Psychoanalytic Study (Chapel Hill: University of North Carolina Press, 1971), Otto Rank stated that, upon using the theme of the double, Poe established a precedent for subsequent treatments. In the foreword to Marie Bonaparte's seminal volume, The Life and Works of Edgar Allan Poe: A Psychoanalytic Interpretation (London: Imago, 1949), Sigmund Freud referred to Poe as “a great writer with pathological trends” (xi). In his collection of seminars, Écrits (London: Tavistock, 1977), Jacques Lacan produced a most influential interpretation of Poe's “The Purloined Letter” to analyze the concept of the symbolic chain. Although critics such as Jean Starobinski in The Living Eye (Cambridge, Mass.: Harvard University Press, 1989) have warned that psychoanalytic criticism has often shown two basic tendencies—on the one hand, the attempt to psychoanalyze authors, and on the other hand, the application of preconceived theoretical assumptions—the framework of psychology and psychoanalysis has always proved particularly fruitful to approach Poe's works. In the introduction to his volume Psychology in Edgar Allan Poe, its editor, Gerardo Del Guercio, who specializes in nineteenth-century American literature, argues that this book arises as a result of his realization that “nothing on Edgar Allan Poe and psychology had come around in many years” (7). All the essays compiled in this volume address psychology, but they also pertain to multifaceted disciplines, ranging from popular culture to comparative studies, while at the same time examining a representative selection of Poe's works. Although each essay presents a diverse degree of complexity, some of these chapters resort to intricate concepts pertaining to psychoanalysis, and so it is implied that the target audience of this book should be somehow familiar with this theoretical discourse. Given the manifold themes tackled in the different chapters, this volume presents no predetermined structure, and in the introduction the editor mentions that the reader need not peruse the chapters in any particular order. Precisely as a result of its manifold themes, this book makes a significant contribution, as not only does it demonstrate the enduring validity of psychology as an effective discourse to reexamine different aspects in Poe's works, but it also contributes to updating this discipline and ratifying it as a valuable framework for contemporary literary studies.In the first chapter of this volume, Karen J. Renner points out that, in the decade of the 1840s, Poe published, on the one hand, his Dupin trilogy, which gave birth to the detective genre, and on the other hand, the stories “The Tell-Tale Heart,” “The Black Cat” and “The Imp of the Perverse,” which consist of three confessional accounts narrated by murderers. These two sets of tales respectively portray the fictional figures of the detective and the killer that contributed to cementing Poe's intrinsic duality. Poe and his detective Dupin turned into prototypes for the criminal profiler, characterized as an individual particularly gifted at gaining insight into the criminal's mindset, precisely owing to the profiler's own moral ambiguity. Likewise, Renner claims that Poe and his tales have left an indelible footprint not only on the way serial killers are depicted in fiction, but also on how actual murderers shape their own identities. Poe paved the way for serial killer fiction, since, although he never wrote about serial killers strictly speaking, central features of serial killer fiction can already be traced back to Poe's tales, namely the killer's capacity to pass unnoticed, the emphasis on deciphering the killer's psyche, and his infamous motif of killing in order to play God. Moreover, the archetypal figure of the morally ambiguous profiler in serial killer fiction can be traced back to Poe's tales, as personified by Dupin. One of the most outstanding ideas that Renner puts forward is that Poe's tales could have provided a framework for actual serial killers, as she identifies a direct correlation between the increase in serial murders reports in the decade of the 1970s and 1980s and Poe's growing popularity at the time. Likewise, she also claims that, when some notorious twenty-century serial killers were in high school, Poe's confessional tales of murder were given unprecedented attention in curricula at the time. Drawing on the theories of Elana Gomel, Deborah Cameron, and Elizabeth Frazer, the author of this chapter argues that serial killers resort to cultural representations to account for their behavior and that, among these culturally constructed representations, might be counted Poe's tales. In order to back up this argument, Renner establishes significant parallelisms between the serial killer Ted Bundy's final confession and that of Poe's murderous narrators, thus reaching the conclusion that Poe's influence extends beyond the fictional to reach the factual.Poe's tales have often been a source of inspiration for psychologists and psychiatrists insofar as his short stories provide insight into the hidden aspects of the human mind. Drawing on David M. Wegner's idea that repressed thoughts turn into obsessions, in the second chapter of this book Rachel McCoppin claims that Poe's narrators repress natural impulses, and in so doing, their unwanted impulses transform into obsessions coming from their unexplored unconscious. In analogy with scholars such as David R. Saliba, Eric W. Carlson, and James Gargano, who approached Poe's works through a psychoanalytic framework, Rachel McCoppin bases her premises on Freud's ideas that fearful impulses arise as a result of restricting the unconscious in an attempt to fit social expectations. In addition, she also resorts to Jung's analytical psychology, which extols the need to examine all aspects of the self, even the dark features of the shadow, since, first, if these fearful emotions are not examined, the individual may project them onto objects or people and may end up turning them into obsessions; and second, these unwanted impulses of the unconscious are often revealing, as they are linked with mortality and are important for psychic growth. Drawing on these notions, McCoppin argues that Poe's narrators refuse to examine their perverse impulses in an attempt to escape death and thus, owing to the Freudian connection between Eros and Thanatos—love and death—Poe's narrators often kill those they love in an attempt to dispel both the fear of their death as well as of their own mortality. Poe's tale “The Imp of the Perverse” is taken as a case in point, since the narrator is reluctant to accept his impulses —and thus his fear of death—which turn into an obsession that can only be quelled by killing the projection of this anxiety, embodied in the man who loves him and also discloses the narrator's own fear of mortality. As McCoppin pertinently demonstrates, this same format displayed in “The Imp of the Perverse” can also be identified in many of Poe's tales featuring obsessive narrators, such as “The Tell-Tale Heart,” “The Black Cat,” “Berenice,” “Morella,” and “William Wilson,” which are all indicative of the obsessions of Poe's narrators as a result of their unwillingness to inspect and accept their unconscious selves.In the third chapter, Sean J. Kelly refers to the usefulness of psychoanalysis to examine the psychological subject but also, most importantly, to analyze how aesthetic effects are generated in Poe's works. In this remarkable essay, which was first published in the Edgar Allan Poe Review in 2016 (“Staging Nothing: The Figure of Das Ding in Poe's ‘The Raven,’” 17, no. 2: 116–41), it is argued that, in Poe's poem “The Raven,” aesthetic effects are produced by a dialectics of presence and absence, through the Freudian-Lacanian concept of das Ding, which is considered as the lost object at the center of our desire, since art creates this void but also introduces the possibility of filling it. In “The Raven,” the speaker grieves for the death of his beloved Lenore, through experiencing the Freudian concept of melancholia, which involves the loss of something which has been withdrawn from consciousness; and it is by staging this void through aesthetic means that the poem examines the melancholic nature of desire. Even if it designates something that is missing, for the subject das Ding implies the mythical state of ontological wholeness from which the subject is deprived upon entering language, so that das Ding marks the void in being itself and, as something familiar which has been repressed, it also turns into an expression of the uncanny. By means of the concept of das Ding, Sean J. Kelly argues that “The Raven” involves Poe's attempt to create the void in art, from the encounter with the uncanny void early on to the sublimation of the raven at the end. In this poem, Poe first resorts to a negative poetics and also displays the incapacity of language to represent the emptiness that allows das Ding to appear as an uncanny presence. Lenore's idealized image functions as a representation as well as a defense against das Ding, since the image of Lenore turns into a reflection of the speaker's desired subjective unity, but her name also arises as an empty signifier that embodies the void itself, so that the encounter with das Ding involves both affect and anxiety. As Sean J. Kelly significantly concludes, Poe finally resorts to a new aesthetic strategy, when idealization transforms into sublimation by means of the repetitive structure of a refrain and the final encounter with the raven. This compulsive repetition, which is reminiscent of Freud's death drive, implies the urge to return to primeval unity, while the raven personifies the sublime by turning into a representative of das Ding—or to use Lacan's terminology, a representative of a representation, which anticipates the nihilistic absurdity of modernism.In the following chapter, Tatiana Prorokova contends that Poe contributed significantly to the development of psychology, since his tales often depict cases of mental disorders and provide clinical presentations, which give evidence of Poe's interest in this medical field and his fascination with the human mind. The author of this chapter claims that Poe considers insanity a result of human fallibility and that sinfulness is an inherent part of the self, while madness often manifests through mental dualism and the dichotomy between goodness and evil. Through an analysis of four of Poe's tales—“The Fall of the House of Usher,” “William Wilson,” “The Tell-Tale Heart,” and “The Black Cat”—Prorokova examines the correlation between madness and sinfulness, as well as the duality of the human mind as embodied in the figure of the doppelgänger. Through a close examination of the mad protagonists in these four stories, it is established that moral sins such as murder, gambling, and alcoholism are reinforced by fits of madness and mental disorders. Likewise, it is also argued that, owing to the dualism of human nature, doppelgängers emerge in Poe's tales to strike a balance between sin and virtue, as they appear when the main character commits a sin and is in need of some moral guidance. Prorokova significantly contends that, in Poe's tales, mental disorders correlate with human depravity, since human nature is split, as shown through the symbolic emergence of the narrator's doppelgänger, which ultimately leads to the narrator's metaphorical suicide as a result of his incapacity to cope with guilt.By means of an analysis of “The Tell-Tale Heart” through the concept of extramission, which links vision and consciousness, Phillip Grayson examines our ethical obligations to fictional beings and our understanding of fictionality. As the author of this chapter argues, “The Tell-Tale Heart” displays three levels of fictiveness: the fictional real, which involves all the characters in the story; the fictional unreal, which is personified by the imagined elderly man before and after his death; and the really real, which revolves around Poe, the author of the story. The relation between the fictional real and the fictional unreal replicates that between the really real and fictional works, and thus, drawing on the theories of Bruno Latour, it is claimed that fictional beings have some exteriority, as they are based on what is real, and they project themselves on us after having imposed themselves on their authors. Through the theory of extramission, it is claimed that vision moves outward from the eyes and projects consciousness through attention; and so by paying attention, our consciousness is projected outside our mind, in the same way that, by paying attention to others, we also presuppose their consciousness. Resorting to the concept of extramission and the analysis of two key images in “The Tell-Tale Heart,” those of the elderly man's eye and beating heart, Phillip Grayson analyzes the relationships between characters and how these fictional beings project themselves on our lives. In “Tell-Tale Heart,” since the elderly man's eye fails to emit his consciousness and to establish his inner reality, for the narrator the elderly man turns into an unreal entity—a result of the narrator's projecting mind—and consequently, the narrator believes he can kill the old man with impunity. Nonetheless, as Grayson further argues, by means of the imaginary beatings of the heart, the narrator feels the ethical obligation to the fictional being in a way that he had not felt for the real old man because of his failure of extramission. Similarly, it is claimed that the ethical obligation that the narrator feels towards the fictional elderly man in the story replicates the same ethical demand that Poe makes on his readers, as both author and audience collaborate to create authorial consciousness, and Poe also intends to survive the death of his “real” self.In the last chapter, written by the editor of this volume, Gerardo Del Guercio claims that Poe adapted the metaphysics and fluent gender boundaries of his works from the German author E. T. A. Hoffmann and, according to German criticism of Poe's writings, this prefigured the concerns of the twentieth century in Poe's works, thus offering a unique reflection of the American mindset at that time. As Del Guercio argues, Hoffmann and German idealism exerted an important influence on Poe's writings, especially in his development of the short story genre, the blurring borders between hyperrational poetics and metaphysical speculations, his interest in the single effect, his creative impulses as a writer and his notion of art as a narcissistic mirror, his emphasis on retreating from the ordinary world, and his critique of the purely materialistic. The author of this chapter pays close attention to the divergent conceptions of otherness that both authors embrace, since Hoffmann considers the double as a pathological estrangement from oneself, whereas Poe rather contends that a fragmentation of the subject becomes superfluous, owing to Poe's own conceptualization of the bi-part soul. According to Del Guercio, in analogy with the idiosyncrasy of Poe's figure of the double, Poe's consideration of the female gender also appears to be more intricate than that of Hoffmann. It is claimed that, for both writers, the spiritual relationships that men establish with women are symptomatic of their incompleteness as men. However, in both cases, women are deprived of their sense of identity, as they remain spiritual entities or signifiers for their male counterparts, and yet, as Del Guercio contends, in contrast with Hoffmann's writings, in Poe's tales women are able to transcend the barriers between life and death.Del Guercio's volume consists of a well-informed collection of essays which draw on the theoretical framework of psychology and psychoanalysis; however, following contemporary trends within this discipline, these essays do not aim to analyze the figure of Poe and his creative genius but rather provide updated reinterpretations of Poe's works by means of this theoretical discourse. One of the main strengths of this book is that it demonstrates psychology and psychoanalysis still prove a valid and effective framework to continue analyzing Poe's tales and poems from manifold perspectives, resorting to canonical theorists such as Freud, Jung, and Lacan to update their theories and shed new light on different aspects of Poe's fiction. Owing to the fact that this volume is a valuable contribution to this tradition, it could have acknowledged some of its most outstanding predecessors such as John P. Muller and William J. Richardson's The Purloined Poe: Lacan, Derrida and Psychoanalytic Reading (Baltimore: Johns Hopkins University Press, 1988), and more recently, Justyna Rusak's Poe and Psychoanalysis: A Critical Overview of the Evolutionary Paths of Psychoanalytic Studies on E. A. Poe (Riga: VDM Verlag Dr. Müller, 2011), which gives evidence of the unrelenting interest in revisiting Poe's works through this theoretical framework in the first decade of the present century. Del Guercio's book is innovative insofar as it manages to intersect psychology as an overall discourse with very different disciplines within literary studies, such as popular culture, aesthetics, poetics, ethics, and comparative literature, while it also bridges the gap between the different genres comprised by Poe's works. Owing to the inherent interdisciplinarity of the volume and given the value of psychoanalytic insights into the structures of language and culture, this book could have benefited from analyses of Poe's works particularly focused on gender and race from a psychoanalytic perspective, while it could also have included essays addressing some of Poe's tales which still have not been granted the attention they truly deserve. In any case, I believe this compilation of critical essays should be heralded as a significant and thought-provoking contemporary contribution to Poe studies from the discourse of psychology, while it also paves the way for subsequent publications aimed at revisiting Poe's works through this mostly productive critical framework.

records.title: Introduction: Feminist Humor and the Future of Fumerism
records.abstract: This special issue on feminist humor looks at the relationship between humor and feminist thought while interrogating the category of female humor itself. The “fumerist,” a term dubbed by comedian Kate Clinton, refers to the feminist humorist who celebrates female difference while expressing underlying feelings of rage.1 Pioneering theorist of feminist humor, Regina Barreca, notes the revolutionary potential of the term “fumerist,” which “captures the idea of being funny and wanting to burn the house down all at once.”2 Seen as too bold, too brainy, too bawdy, and too bitchy, feminist humorists have been overlooked and resisted by predominantly male critics, saddled by their misconceptions of what constitutes “female” behavior and what is worthy of laughter.3The idea that women were not supposed to get a joke, let alone tell one, is rooted in the perception of the second-wave feminist commitment to advancing gender equality through political, legal and social action as no laughing matter. Sara Ahmed among others exposes this fallacy with her concept of the feminist killjoy, who challenges patriarchal authority through joyful resistance and has fun doing so.4 The use of irony, satire, parody, and wit as masked forms of social critique in the US dates back to nineteenth-century female humorists like Fanny Fern (Sara Willis Parton), Frances Miriam Whitcher, and Marietta Holley, who used humor to challenge gender norms, and early twentieth-century writers like Carolyn Wells, Alice Duer Miller, and Florence Guy Seabury, who used it to critique the patriarchal power structure and advocate for women’s suffrage and women’s rights more broadly. In their reappraisal of the “fumerist,” Cynthia Willett and Julie Willett emphasize the affective power of feminist laughter, how moving beyond the rational power of thought to the “biosocial and psychosocial” power of the “belly laugh” has “cathartic effects of an erotic politics of laughter” rooted in pleasure and joy. In asserting the joy as well as the fury of feminist laughter, contemporary feminist humorists seek to build “mutual communities of belonging” and “unexpected alliances” that hold promise for the future of fumerism.5Since the publication of the last special issue of Studies in American Humor dedicated to “women’s humor” in 2011, “Funny Girls: Humor and American Women Writers,” much has changed in the cultural landscape in relation to issues of social justice as well as humor studies. Advocacy for gender and racial equality and female reproductive rights has been renewed with the advent of the #MeToo, #TimesUp, #BlackLivesMatter, and #SayHerName movements and the overturning of Roe v. Wade. The expansion of new media platforms has also led to a renaissance of feminist humor that has in turn impacted humor studies. While the previous issue on female humor was largely focused on literary humor, scholarship today explores a variety of genres from satire and parody to stand-up, sketch comedy, television, film, and cartoons as well as digital media.While the label “women’s humor” can be useful, it has its limitations, and it is a fluid term that has changed meaning over time. In the 1970s, ’80s, and early ’90s in the wake of second-wave feminism and the women’s movement, the study of women’s humor was inaugurated with the publication of pioneering works by Nancy A. Walker, Regina Barreca, Emily Toth, Judy Little, and Linda A. Morris as well as important collections of essays on women’s humor edited by Barreca, Morris, Gail Finney, and June Sochen.6 The valuable anthologies of primary source material by female humorists including Martha Bensley Bruère and Mary Ritter Beard’s historic collection, Laughing Their Way: Women’s Humor in America (1934), Nancy Walker and Zita Dresner’s Redressing the Balance: American Women’s Literary Humor from Colonial Times to the 1980s (1988), and Daryl Cumber Dance’s Honey Hush!: An Anthology of African Women’s Humor (1998) further showed that women’s humor was a serious field of study.7 While these authors made groundbreaking contributions to the field, their work often reflects the second-wave feminist emphasis on reviving and uncovering works by and about women and has been criticized by some as reinforcing an essentialist, largely white, heteronormative, cisgendered point of view. Emphasizing the existence of a unique category of women’s humor can result in the minimalization of differences of race, class, gender, sexuality, ability, and national origin among types of women’s humor as well as the affinity between humor by women and by those from other marginalized groups, regardless of gender. Such categories of male and female humor have been increasingly troubled by our understanding of gender queer or nonbinary humor production.More recent multidisciplinary and intersectional approaches to feminist humor include works by Maggie Hennefeld and Kristen Anderson Wagner that focus on film, Michelle Ann Abate’s contribution to the study of comics, Jenny Sundén and Susanna Paasonen’s focus on feminist humor and social media, Shawn Levy’s study on stand-up comedians, works by Lisa A. Guerrero and Danielle Fuentes Morgan on African American satire and by Katelyn Hale Wood on Black feminist comedy, and Rebecca Krefting’s work on “charged” humor.8 Scholarship that explores feminist literary humor through an intersectional lens includes Margaret D. Stetz’s on the literary parody of transatlantic female humorists of the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, Rachel Trousdale’s and Calista McRae’s on humor in poetry, and my own on female humorists’ use of satire, irony, and wit in the interwar period.9 Current collections of essays on feminist humor and humor in general take a more intersectional approach and raise questions about the intention as well as the efficacy of humor, asking to what extent humor can or should translate into political action and social change.10Early resistance to feminist humor on the grounds that women aren’t funny is laughable given the proliferation of women’s humor and an awareness of the sexist origins of such claims. The idea that women aren’t funny is rooted in false binary oppositions between masculinity/femininity, intellect/emotion, aggression/submission, sexuality/purity, funny/pretty that reinforce an outdated Victorian ideal of the “cult of True Womanhood” based in “piety, purity, submissiveness, and domesticity.” According to Barreca, this split creates a double bind for women between the “good girl,” who doesn’t swear, tell jokes, or engage in sexual or aggressive behavior, and the “bad girl,” who does all of the above. “Learning to sound like a Good Girl, while half-concealing the text of the Bad Girl,” Barreca argues, “has been the subject of a great deal of women’s humor” (They Used to Call Me Snow White . . . but I Drifted, 16). Female humorists often mask this subversive or underlying meaning by invoking gender stereotypes in order to subvert them. According to Walker, many critics fail to recognize humor by women and other marginalized groups “largely because the use of stereotypes is assumed to constitute an acceptance of that stereotype” (A Very Serious Thing, 20). Female humorists often “employ stereotypes of women”—which include “the gossipy spinster, the nagging wife, the inept housekeeper, the lovelorn woman, the dumb blond”—“for the purpose of mocking those stereotypes and showing their absurdity and even danger,” Walker states. (9–11). Humorists’ negative use of gender and racial stereotypes is at times so concealed (or the assumption of stereotypes by the reader/audience so strong) that the use can be misinterpreted as an unironic endorsement of such biased norms.While popular theories of humor can be limiting, they can help provide a framework through which we can examine the evolving field of feminist humor. According to an outmoded but nonetheless influential relief theory of humor as elaborated by Freud, “tendentious jokes,” or jokes with purpose, are an outlet for hostile or obscene thoughts and feelings that are temporarily uninhibited and released through laughter.11 These jokes are often used by those in positions of greater authority with the purpose of insulting those in subordinate positions, or “punching down,” thereby reinforcing the status quo. Since these aggressive and sexual tendencies were seen as “unfeminine,” it followed that women were not or should not be the initiators of laughter. Outspoken women of intellect and wit were demonized by a false dichotomy between the domestic “angel” and the liberated “monster.”12 According to Hélène Cixous, this defiant laughter is a matter of perception and can be seen as empowering or threatening depending on your point of view. “You only have to look at the Medusa straight to see her. And she’s not deadly. She’s beautiful and she’s laughing.”13 This type of laughter stands in contrast to the “faked” laughter of a woman at a man’s joke of which she or some other subordinate person is the butt and can be seen as a physical release, like a kind of orgasm, especially when originated by a woman. But it can also be seen as an assertion of female sexuality, knowledge, and ultimately power. The laughing Medusa, says feminist theorist Susan Rubin Suleiman, is a “trope for women’s autonomous subjectivity and for the necessary irreverence of women’s writing and rewriting.”14 The relation of humor to knowledge and of knowledge to power is at the root of the female claim to humor and the denial, especially among male critics, of feminist humor.The incongruity theory of humor, with its emphasis on the verbal presentation and cognitive perception of a double or ironic meaning (of a socially accepted overt and an underlying subversive meaning), has been central to an understanding of feminist humor. Unlike the relief theory and the superiority-disparagement theories of humor, which emphasize the sexual/aggressive tendencies and the social nature of humor, the incongruity theory is more cognitively oriented, based on the perceptual and verbal aspects of humor, in particular in the use of irony and wit. Incongruity theory is based on the “assumption that human experience works with learned patterns and expectations. When a thing violates our expectation or mental pattern, it is incongruous.”15 This approach can be traced back to Aristotle, who identifies laughter as being caused by a violation of expectation, and Immanuel Kant, who famously defines it as “an affection arising from the sudden transformation of a strained expectation into nothing.”16The “double-voiced discourse” commonly found in feminist humor also reflects what Mikhail Bakhtin refers to as “heteroglossia” or the “dialogic” voice found in “the Menippea” (Menippean satire), which, according to Bakhtin, displays “dialogical parody.”17 While
